opus-5.5.text:
I think the core difference is in what people actually bring to it. With a chatbot, the interaction is fundamentally conversational. You ask a question, you get an answer, and a huge fraction of usage ends up being things like "help me write this," "explain this concept," or honestly just chatting. The cost of a bad answer is low, and the user stays in the loop the whole time, reading every line.

Operator is different because it's an agent that acts. You're not asking it to tell you something, you're asking it to do something: book a restaurant, fill out a form, buy a ticket, go through a website and get a task finished. So the kinds of requests people send are much more goal-oriented and much more concrete. And that changes the psychology on both sides.

For the user, there's a delegation mindset. You hand off the task and you want to come back to a result. That means the tolerance for errors is much lower. If a chatbot gives a slightly off paragraph, you just edit it. If an agent clicks the wrong button and books the wrong date or pays for the wrong thing, that's a real-world consequence. So trust becomes the central issue, not just intelligence.

For the system, that means the training objective is quite different too. In chat, you can optimize a lot around human preference: is this response helpful, is it pleasant, is it well written. With an agent, what matters is whether the task actually got done, over many steps, in a messy environment like real web pages that change, that have pop-ups, logins, captchas. That's much closer to a reinforcement learning problem in the classic sense: long horizon, sparse reward, and you have to recover from your own mistakes along the way.

There's also an interaction pattern question that I find really interesting. A good agent needs to know when to stop and ask. If it asks too often, it's annoying and you might as well do it yourself. If it never asks, it'll do something you didn't want, like entering payment information or making an irreversible choice. So calibrating that boundary, when to be autonomous and when to hand control back to the human, is something ordinary chatbots basically never had to deal with.

So I'd say Operator attracts a different kind of user intent: less "talk to me," more "do this for me." And once you move into "do this for me," everything changes: the evaluation, the safety considerations, the product design, and the underlying RL training. That's why I see agents as a genuinely new stage rather than just a chatbot with a few extra tools attached.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the thing about Operator is that it actually goes out and does things in the browser for you. It's an agent, not a chatbot. And once a product can act, the way people approach it changes completely.

With a chatbot, the interaction is bounded by the conversation itself. You ask, it answers. If the answer is bad, you shrug and rephrase. The cost of a mistake is basically zero, so people treat it like a toy or a search engine. Very low stakes, very casual.

With Operator, people show up with a task that has a real outcome attached. Book this flight. Order these groceries. Fill out this form. So first, the intent is much more concrete and goal-directed. Users aren't exploring, they're delegating. And second, the tolerance for error is totally different, because now a mistake means money spent on the wrong thing, or a reservation at the wrong restaurant. That raises the bar for reliability enormously, and it also raises the bar for trust. You have to be willing to hand over your logged-in accounts, your payment info, your personal context.

So the kinds of users it attracts are people who already know exactly what they want done and are willing to let a system act on their behalf. That's a much narrower, but much more valuable, interaction. And I think it's also why the early experience feels rough. The chatbot form factor lets the model hide behind language. An agent in a browser can't hide. Every click is visible, every hesitation is visible, and the user is sitting there judging whether this thing is competent enough to be trusted with their stuff.

From a research point of view that's actually the interesting part. Those interactions generate a completely different signal than chat logs. You get to see where the model gets stuck in a real environment, where it misunderstands a goal, where a human has to step in. That's exactly the kind of data you need to make agents better, and you simply don't get it from a conversation box.

astra-6.text:
I think the key difference is that an ordinary chatbot invites you to ask, “What can you tell me?” Operator invites you to ask, “What can you do for me?” That changes the interaction from getting an answer to delegating a task.

With a chatbot, you might ask how to book a trip. With Operator, you might ask it to work through the booking process. Then the conversation becomes about your preferences, missing information, and which decisions need your confirmation. The answer itself is no longer the whole product; what matters is whether the task gets completed correctly.

That also changes the trust you need. You can read a chatbot’s advice before acting on it. When an agent acts on your behalf, you need to understand what it’s doing and have a way to intervene.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key difference is that with an ordinary chatbot, you’re mostly asking it to tell you something. With Operator, you’re asking it to do something. That changes the interaction from a question and an answer into a task: here’s my goal, here are my preferences, go work through the steps.

And once you ask a system to act, the conversation naturally becomes more about delegation. What can it decide by itself? When should it come back and ask you? How do you check that it actually accomplished what you wanted? So the interesting difference isn’t just the interface. It’s the kind of relationship the user is trying to have with the system—from getting advice to handing off work.
